The final optimized nacelle design achieved a cruise drag of 26.9 drag counts.
The bypass nozzle of the optimized design had a maximum velocity coefficient (Cv) of 0.9914 and a discharge coefficient (Cd) of 0.995.
The intake pressure recovery (IPR) of the optimized designs was in the range of 0.9975-0.9985 at cruise conditions.
The loop2 optimized design had a mass flow capture ratio (MFCR) of 0.68, lower than the 0.75 for the loop1 design.
The loop2 design had a higher contraction ratio (CR) of 1.34 compared to 1.24 for the loop1 design.
The loop2 design had a 50% higher leading edge radius of curvature (R_LE) compared to the loop1 design.
The loop2 design showed significantly better crosswind performance, with a DC60 value of -0.015 at 30 knots crosswind, compared to -0.411 for the loop1 design.
The intake throat Mach number had an almost linear inverse proportional relationship with the throat radius.
Longer intake lengths were found to improve the intake diffusion factor by allowing for greater flow deceleration.
The position of maximum nacelle diameter (f_max) had a significant impact on external drag, with an optimum around f_max = 0.35.
The decoupled optimization approach assumed minimal aerodynamic interactions between the intake-fan cowl and bypass duct-nozzle systems.
The iCST parameterization provided better control over the nacelle geometry compared to ellipse or B-spline methods.
The adaptive response surface methodology optimization algorithm allowed for efficient exploration of the design space.
No shocks were present within the intake for the range of designs evaluated, as the average throat Mach number remained below 0.8.
The loop2 design had a higher margin for an increase in intake mass flow before any internal shocks would occur, with a peak Mach number of 0.8 at the throat.
